title: SOC Foundations

theory.concept: A Security Operations Centre runs a queue. Detections arrive from many sensors (SIEM correlation rules, EDR, firewall, mail gateway), land in a triage queue, and a Tier-1 analyst decides in minutes what each one is: real (True Positive), noise (False Positive), or something that needs a more senior analyst (Escalation). Nothing else in this platform makes sense until queue discipline does.
theory.why: Queue order decides which incident is contained first. An analyst who works top-to-bottom instead of by risk lets a critical detection sit while a low-value informational alert is written up.
look: Severity of the detection combined with the business value of the asset it fired on
Whether the same rule has fired repeatedly on the same host (possible noise or possible campaign)
Assets that are domain controllers, file servers or finance endpoints - these outrank a lab VM
Alerts with a status of NEW and no owner - unowned critical alerts are the real risk
Detections that reference external source addresses at unusual hours
fp: A high-severity rule firing on a decommissioned or test host is often noise
A scheduled vulnerability scanner will trip dozens of rules every week and is authorised
tips: Read the asset inventory before ranking the queue
Severity in the tool is only a suggestion - asset criticality changes the ranking

title: Security Events

theory.concept: Every operating system writes structured records of security-relevant actions. Windows uses numeric Event IDs in the Security channel; Linux writes text lines to auth.log or the journal; network devices emit their own formats. Reading these natively - without a pretty dashboard in front of you - is the single most portable SOC skill there is.
theory.why: SIEM field names change between vendors. Event ID 4624 does not. An analyst who knows the raw event meaning can work in any environment on day one.
look: 4624 successful logon, 4625 failed logon, 4634 logoff, 4740 account lockout, 4720 account created, 4732 member added to a security-enabled local group
4688 process creation - the parent process field is usually more interesting than the child
Logon Type: 2 interactive at keyboard, 3 network, 10 RemoteInteractive (RDP), 5 service, 4 batch
Linux: 'Accepted password', 'Failed password', 'session opened for user', sudo COMMAND entries
Status/sub-status codes on 4625 - 0xC000006A is a bad password, 0xC0000064 is a username that does not exist
fp: Service accounts generate huge volumes of Type 5 and Type 3 logons legitimately
A user who changed their password will produce a short burst of 4625s from cached credentials on phones and mapped drives
tips: A 4625 storm made of 0xC0000064 means the attacker is guessing usernames, not passwords
4740 tells you the lockout threshold was reached - useful for counting attempts you cannot see

title: Alert Triage

theory.concept: Triage is the decision layer between detection and investigation. For each alert the analyst answers three questions: is the observed behaviour real, is it authorised, and does it warrant escalation. Most enterprise SOCs run a False Positive rate above 50 percent - correctly closing noise is as valuable as catching attacks, because it buys back the time needed for real work.
theory.why: An analyst who escalates everything destroys Tier 2 capacity. An analyst who closes everything misses the breach. Evidence-backed closure is the skill.
look: A matching entry in the change calendar or deployment tooling
The process signer and the path it executed from - C:\\Windows\\CCM or a signed vendor agent is very different from C:\\Users\\Public
Whether the same activity appears identically across many hosts at the same minute (that pattern means software deployment, not intrusion)
The account driving the activity - SYSTEM under a management agent versus a normal user account
fp: Software deployment tools legitimately spawn PowerShell, msiexec and remote service installs on hundreds of endpoints
Security products themselves (EDR, backup agents, DLP) trigger behavioural rules constantly
tips: Never close an alert on a feeling. Close it on a named artefact: a change ID, a signature, a deployment job number.
If the behaviour is identical on 60 hosts within 4 minutes, look for the orchestration server before you look for an attacker.

title: Authentication Analysis

theory.concept: Authentication attacks come in three shapes. Brute force hammers one account with many passwords. Password spraying tries one common password across many accounts to stay under the lockout threshold. Credential stuffing replays username/password pairs stolen elsewhere. All three look the same at first glance and are separated by the ratio of accounts to attempts.
theory.why: Valid credentials are the cheapest way into an enterprise. Almost every major intrusion has an authentication event at its root, and it is almost always visible in logs before anything else happens.
look: A run of 4625 failures followed by a 4624 success from the same source address
Same source, many usernames = spraying or enumeration; same username, many attempts = brute force
Logon Type 3 (network) from an address that is not in any office range
Time of day: successful authentication at 02:00 for an account that only ever works 09:00-17:00
What happened in the 10 minutes AFTER the success - that is where the intrusion actually starts
fp: A user returning from leave with an expired password generates failure bursts
A service account with a rotated password will fail repeatedly from every server that still caches the old one - the giveaway is that the source addresses are internal servers, not one external IP
tips: Count the failures precisely. The count is evidence and will go into the incident report.
The first suspicious event and the last suspicious event define the attack window you will hand to Tier 2.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 - SOC Analyst ka Role
chapters.body: SOC (Security Operations Centre) ek team hoti hai jo organization ke systems ko 24/7 monitor karti hai. Tier-1 SOC Analyst is team ka wo insaan hai jo sab se pehle alert dekhta hai. Aap ka kaam sirf 'panic button' dabana nahi, balki har alert ko evidence ke sath verify karna hai.
chapters.example: Misal ke taur par, agar aap ko ek alert milta hai 'Multiple Failed Logins on DC-01', to aap ka kaam yeh nahi ke foran host ko band kar dein - balki pehle logs padh kar confirm karein ke kya waqai koi attack ho raha hai.
chapters.lookFor: SOC Analyst ko dekhna chahiye: alert ka time, affected host/account, aur kya yeh pattern pehle bhi dekha gaya hai.
chapters.mistake: Common mistake: sirf alert ki severity label dekh kar decision le lena, evidence ko detail mein na padhna.
chapters.practical: Agla case shuru karne se pehle socho: agar aap ki shift shuru hoti hai aur queue mein 5 alerts hain, aap sab se pehle konsa kholenge aur kyun?

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - Alerts kya hotay hain?
chapters.body: Alert ka matlab ek aisi notification hai jo security system (SIEM, EDR, firewall) generate karta hai jab koi unusual ya potentially suspicious activity detect hoti hai. Har alert ek 'suggestion' hai, hukum nahi - is liye analyst ko verify karna zaroori hai.
chapters.example: Ek SIEM rule 'Multiple failed logons (>5) single source' fire hoti hai jab ek hi source se paanch se zyada failed login attempts ek chhoti si window mein aa jayein.
chapters.lookFor: Alert ke andar rule name, severity, host, account aur count field dekhein - yeh sab milkar batatay hain ke alert ka scope kya hai.
chapters.mistake: Har alert ko attack samajh lena. Har alert attack nahi hota - SOC analyst ka kaam evidence verify karna hai, sirf alert dekh kar reaction dena nahi.
chapters.practical: Socho: ek alert 'severity=HIGH' hai lekin host ek disconnected test VM hai. Kya yeh phir bhi HIGH priority hai?

chapters.title: Chapter 3 - Authentication aur Login Monitoring
chapters.body: Authentication wo process hai jis mein user apni identity prove karta hai (username + password, ya token). Har login attempt - chahe successful ho ya failed - ek log event banata hai. In events ko monitor karna SOC ka bunyadi kaam hai.
chapters.example: Windows par 'Failed Login' ka matlab hai EventID 4625, aur 'Successful Login' ka matlab hai EventID 4624. Linux par 'Failed password' aur 'Accepted password' lines auth.log mein milti hain.
chapters.lookFor: Dekhna yeh hai: kitni baar login fail hua, konsa account target hua, aur us ke baad koi success hui ya nahi.
chapters.mistake: Sirf failed logins ginna aur yeh bhool jana ke us ke baad kya hua - agar success ho gayi to yeh sirf 'attempt' nahi balki 'compromise' ban jata hai.
chapters.practical: Agar ek account par 12 failed attempts ke baad ek success ho, is se aap kya nateeja nikalenge?

chapters.title: Chapter 4 - Brute Force, Password Spraying aur Credential Stuffing
chapters.body: In teenon attacks ka concept alag hai lekin log mein pehli nazar mein ek jaisay lagtay hain. BRUTE FORCE: ek account, bohat se passwords try kiye jatay hain. PASSWORD SPRAYING: bohat se accounts, ek common password try kiya jata hai (taake lockout se bacha ja sake). CREDENTIAL STUFFING: kahin aur se churaye gaye username/password pairs ko replay kiya jata hai.
chapters.example: Agar log mein sirf 'svc_backup' account par 12 alag attempts hain, ek hi source se - yeh brute force hai. Agar 40 alag accounts par sirf ek hi password try ho raha hai - yeh spraying hai.
chapters.lookFor: Accounts-to-attempts ka ratio dekhein: ek account + kai attempts = brute force. Kai accounts + ek jaisa pattern = spraying.
chapters.mistake: Teeno attacks ko 'brute force' keh dena bina ratio dekhe - yeh galat classification decision aur wrong severity de sakta hai.
chapters.practical: Agar ek hi IP se 5 different accounts par sirf ek attempt each ho, kya yeh brute force hai ya spraying?

chapters.title: Chapter 5 - Authentication Logs Padhna (Windows aur Linux)
chapters.body: Windows Security log mein important Event IDs: 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4634 (logoff), 4740 (account lockout), 4672 (special privileges assigned). Logon Type field bhi zaroori hai: Type 2 = interactive (keyboard par), Type 3 = network, Type 10 = RDP.
chapters.example: 'EventID=4625 SourceIP=203.0.113.55 SubStatus=0xC000006A' ka matlab hai galat password ke sath login fail hua us IP se.
chapters.lookFor: SubStatus code dekhein - 0xC000006A = bad password, 0xC0000064 = username hi exist nahi karta (yeh username enumeration ka sign hai).
chapters.mistake: SubStatus code ko ignore kar dena - yeh bata sakta hai ke attacker sirf guess kar raha hai ya usay pehle se sahi username maloom hai.
chapters.practical: Agar SubStatus 0xC0000064 baar baar different usernames ke sath aaye, aap is se kya samjhenge?

chapters.title: Chapter 6 - Source IP aur Target Account
chapters.body: Source IP wo address hai jahan se login attempt aaya. Target account wo hai jis par attempt hua. In dono ko cross-reference karna zaroori hai: kya source IP normal hai us account ke liye? Kya account ka normal working hours match karta hai attempt ke time se?
chapters.example: Agar 'svc_backup' account normally sirf internal backup server (10.20.8.10) se login karta hai, lekin ab external IP (203.0.113.55) se attempt ho raha hai - yeh ek bara red flag hai.
chapters.lookFor: Account context data mein normal_sources aur normal_hours fields dekhein, phir unko current evidence ke sath compare karein.
chapters.mistake: Sirf IP ko 'external hai isliye bad hai' keh dena bina yeh check kiye ke account ka legitimate use case kya hai.
chapters.practical: Ek user apni normal working hours ke bahar (raat 2 baje) login karta hai - kya yeh apne aap suspicious hai, ya context chahiye?

chapters.title: Chapter 7 - Asset Criticality
chapters.body: Har host ka business mein kitna 'weight' hai, yeh Asset Criticality kehlata hai. Ek Domain Controller (DC), jahan sari organization ki identities store hoti hain, ek lab test VM se kahin zyada critical hai - chahe dono par ek jaisi alert fire ho.
chapters.example: Asset Inventory mein 'DC-01 tier=0 criticality=CRITICAL' likha ho to iska matlab hai ke is host par koi bhi suspicious activity turant Tier-2 ko escalate honi chahiye.
chapters.lookFor: Asset inventory se role, tier aur criticality field check karein - yeh severity decision ko directly affect karta hai.
chapters.mistake: Har host ko ek jaisa treat karna. Tier-0 aur Tier-3 (jaise sandbox lab VM) par same alert ka response same nahi hona chahiye.
chapters.practical: Agar ek hi tarah ka alert DC-01 aur ek lab VM par aaye, dono ki severity same honi chahiye ya alag?

chapters.title: Chapter 8 - Timeline Analysis
chapters.body: Timeline banane ka matlab hai evidence ko waqt (time) ke hisab se order mein lagana taake poori kahani samajh aa sake - shuru se le kar akhri suspicious event tak.
chapters.example: 02:14:02 pehli failed attempt, 02:15:39 success, 02:16:10 privileges assigned, 02:18:44 file share access - yeh timeline batati hai ke attack sirf login tak mehdood nahi, balki us ke baad bhi activity hui.
chapters.lookFor: Sirf 'jab attack shuru hua' nahi balki 'attack kab tak jari raha' bhi dekhein - success ke baad ki activity aksar sab se zyada important hoti hai.
chapters.mistake: Timeline ko successful login par rok dena, jabke asal kahani usse aagay chalti hai.
chapters.practical: Agar login success ke 30 second baad file share access ho, kya yeh coincidence hai ya connected activity?

chapters.title: Chapter 9 - False Positive vs True Positive
chapters.body: TRUE POSITIVE: alert asal mein malicious ya unauthorized activity ko represent karta hai. FALSE POSITIVE: alert fire hui lekin activity legitimate thi (jaise scheduled scan, ya user ka apna password bhool jana).
chapters.example: Agar failed logins ek approved vulnerability scan (change calendar mein documented) se match karte hain, to yeh False Positive hai. Agar external, undocumented IP se attempts aa rahe hain jin ke baad success ho, yeh True Positive hai.
chapters.lookFor: Change calendar aur SOP hamesha check karein - kai 'suspicious' events asal mein authorized activity hoti hain.
chapters.mistake: Har suspicious-looking pattern ko turant True Positive keh dena bina authorization records check kiye.
chapters.practical: Ek vulnerability scanner IP se 200+ 'failed login' type alerts aayein - kya yeh automatically True Positive hai?

chapters.title: Chapter 10 - Change Calendar aur Authorized Activity
chapters.body: Change Calendar wo record hai jahan organization apne planned changes, scans, aur maintenance windows likhti hai. Yeh SOC analyst ka sabse pehla reference point hona chahiye jab koi activity 'unusual' lage.
chapters.example: 'CHG-4471: Authorised credentialed vulnerability scan of DMZ from 10.10.9.15, approved by AppOps' - agar evidence isi IP aur time window se match kare, to activity authorized hai.
chapters.lookFor: Time window, source IP/system, aur approval ka match dekhein - teeno match hone chahiye, sirf ek nahi.
chapters.mistake: Sirf yeh dekh kar ke 'kuch scan jaisa activity hai' foran False Positive keh dena bina change record se confirm kiye.
chapters.practical: Agar activity ka time change window se bahar ho lekin source IP wahi ho jo authorized scanner ka hai, kya yeh phir bhi authorized hai?

chapters.title: Chapter 11 - Escalation aur Analyst Notes
chapters.body: Escalation ka matlab hai case ko Tier-2 ya senior analyst tak bhejna jab woh Tier-1 ke scope se bahar ho (jaise Tier-0 asset compromise). Achay Analyst Notes mein likha hona chahiye: kya hua, kab hua, konsa user/host/IP involved tha, evidence kya hai, activity authorized thi ya nahi, impact/risk kya hai, aur kya action liya gaya.
chapters.example: Ek achi note: 'svc_backup account par 12 failed attempts 203.0.113.55 se, phir success 02:15:39 par. FW-LEGACY-11 rule ne yeh allow kiya. Tier-2 ko escalate kiya gaya SOP-12 ke tehat.'
chapters.lookFor: Notes mein specific evidence cite karein (timestamps, IDs) - sirf 'suspicious activity dekhi' likhna kaafi nahi.
chapters.mistake: Vague notes likhna jaise 'kuch ajeeb hua, escalate kar diya' - is se agle analyst ko kuch pata nahi chalta.
chapters.practical: Apni notes mein kam az kam yeh 5 cheezain zaroor shamil karo: what, when, who/where, evidence, action.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 - Complete Investigation Workflow
chapters.body: Har investigation isi tarteeb se chalti hai: ALERT -> VALIDATE -> IDENTIFY ASSET -> CHECK EVIDENCE -> CORRELATE EVENTS -> CHECK CHANGE/MAINTENANCE -> TRUE POSITIVE/FALSE POSITIVE -> ASSESS RISK -> CONTAINMENT/ESCALATION -> DOCUMENT. Yeh workflow yaad rakho - har case, chahe koi bhi topic ho, isi structure mein follow hoga.
chapters.example: 'Multiple Failed Logins' case mein: Alert padha -> Windows Security log se validate kiya -> DC-01 ko asset inventory mein check kiya (Tier-0) -> 4625/4624 events dekhe -> source IP aur account correlate kiya -> change calendar check kiya (kuch match nahi) -> True Positive decide kiya -> CRITICAL severity di -> Tier-2 escalate kiya -> notes likhi.
chapters.lookFor: Har step ko order mein follow karo - koi step skip mat karo, warna galat decision ban sakta hai.
chapters.mistake: Seedha evidence dekh kar decision de dena, beech ke steps (jaise change calendar check) skip kar dena.
chapters.practical: Ab tum ready ho Knowledge Test dene ke liye. Test mein 10 sawalat aayenge - pass hone ke liye 10/10 chahiye.

quizBank.q: Windows Event ID 4625 kis cheez ko represent karta hai?
quizBank.explain: 4625 hamesha ek FAILED logon attempt ko record karta hai. Successful logon ke liye EventID 4624 hota hai.

quizBank.q: Windows Event ID 4624 kis cheez ko represent karta hai?
quizBank.explain: 4624 ek SUCCESSFUL logon ko record karta hai - yeh sab se important event hota hai jab pehle failures ke baad aata hai.

quizBank.q: Ek hi account par bohat se different passwords try karne ko kya kehte hain?
quizBank.explain: Brute force mein attacker ek target account ko bohat se passwords se guess karne ki koshish karta hai.

quizBank.q: Ek hi common password ko bohat se different accounts par try karne ko kya kehte hain (lockout se bachne ke liye)?
quizBank.explain: Password spraying mein attacker jaan bujh kar sirf 1-2 password try karta hai har account par, taake lockout threshold cross na ho.

quizBank.q: SubStatus 0xC000006A ka matlab kya hai?
quizBank.explain: 0xC000006A ka matlab hai username sahi hai lekin password ghalat diya gaya - yeh password guessing ka sign hai.

quizBank.q: SubStatus 0xC0000064 ka matlab kya hai?
quizBank.explain: 0xC0000064 batata hai ke diya gaya username hi system mein exist nahi karta - baar baar aana username enumeration ka sign hai.

quizBank.q: Logon Type 3 ka matlab kya hai?
quizBank.explain: Type 3 ek network logon hoti hai (jaise SMB share access) - keyboard par direct login nahi.

quizBank.q: Agar ek service account normally sirf internal backup server se login karta hai, lekin ab ek external IP se login attempt aa raha hai, yeh kya indicate karta hai?
quizBank.explain: Account context (normal_sources) se mismatch hamesha investigate karna chahiye - yeh compromise ka strong indicator hai.

quizBank.q: SOC mein 'Change Calendar' check karne ka maqsad kya hai?
options: Authorized activity ko unauthorized se separate karna
quizBank.explain: Change calendar SOC ko batata hai ke koi activity pehle se approved/planned thi ya nahi - is se False Positive jaldi identify hota hai.

quizBank.q: Agar failed login attempts bilkul us waqt match karte hain jab ek approved vulnerability scan chal raha tha, decision kya hoga?
quizBank.explain: Jab evidence documented, approved change ke sath match kare, to yeh False Positive hai - real threat nahi.

quizBank.q: Asset criticality kis field se pata chalti hai?
quizBank.explain: Asset inventory record (tier, criticality, owner) yeh batata hai ke host business ke liye kitna important hai - yeh severity decision ko directly influence karta hai.

quizBank.q: Ek Domain Controller (DC) ka asset tier aam tor par kya hota hai?
quizBank.explain: Domain Controllers Tier-0 assets hain kyun ke wahan poori organization ki identities store hoti hain - inka compromise sab se zyada khatarnak hota hai.

quizBank.q: Attack timeline banate waqt sab se badi ghalti kya hoti hai?
options: Successful login ke baad ki activity ko ignore karna
quizBank.explain: Bohat se analysts timeline ko success tak seedh dete hain, jabke asal kahani (jaise privilege escalation, file access) usse aagay hoti hai.

quizBank.q: 'Needs Escalation' decision kab select karni chahiye?
options: Jab evidence bilkul clear False Positive ho
Jab case Tier-1 ke scope se bahar ho ya Tier-0 asset involve ho
Jab investigation abhi shuru hui ho
Kabhi nahi, hamesha khud close karna chahiye
quizBank.explain: Agar case mein Tier-0 asset involve ho ya scope Tier-1 se bara ho, SOP ke mutabiq Tier-2 ko escalate karna chahiye.

quizBank.q: Ek achi Analyst Note mein kaunsi cheez zaroor honi chahiye?
options: Specific evidence, timestamps aur action liya gaya
Kuch bhi nahi, sirf decision kaafi hai
quizBank.explain: Achi notes specific hoti hain: what happened, when, evidence (timestamps/IDs), aur kya action liya gaya - taake agla analyst turant samajh sake.

quizBank.q: EventID 4740 kis cheez ko represent karta hai?
quizBank.explain: 4740 batata hai ke ek account lockout threshold reach hone ki waja se lock ho gaya - yeh un attempts ka proxy ho sakta hai jo aap ne khud nahi dekhe.

quizBank.q: Credential stuffing kis cheez par based hota hai?
options: Pehle se churaye gaye username/password pairs replay karna
Sirf ek hi common password try karna
quizBank.explain: Credential stuffing mein attacker kisi aur breach se churaye gaye asal username/password combinations ko yahan try karta hai.

quizBank.q: EventID 4672 kis waqt generate hota hai?
options: Jab account ko special privileges assign hon
quizBank.explain: 4672 tab record hota hai jab kisi account ko special/administrative privileges assign ki jayein - yeh privilege escalation ka indicator ho sakta hai.

quizBank.q: Agar attack window ke baad attacker ADMIN$ share access karta hai, is se kya pata chalta hai?
options: Attack sirf login tak mehdood tha
Attacker ne login ke baad bhi activity ki - severity barh sakti hai
quizBank.explain: Login ke baad share access ya privilege use, batata hai ke attacker ne successful access ko actively istemal kiya - is se severity aur bhi barh jati hai.

quizBank.q: Tier-1 SOC Analyst ka bunyadi kaam kya hai?
options: Har alert ko turant block kar dena
Evidence verify karke sahi decision (TP/FP/Escalation) lena
Passwords khud reset karna bina kisi verification ke
quizBank.explain: Tier-1 analyst ka kaam evidence ko dhyan se verify karna aur sahi classification (True Positive / False Positive / Needs Escalation) dena hai - panic ya guess nahi.

steps.title: Step 1 - Alert Padho
steps.ask: Neeche diya gaya alert ghoor kar parho: 'Multiple failed logons (>6) single source, no subsequent success' - WKS-3502 par.
steps.why: Har investigation ka pehla kaam hai alert ko samajhna - yeh kya keh raha hai, konsa host, konsa pattern.
steps.reveal: Yeh alert bata raha hai: (1) ek hi source se (2) 6 se zyada failed attempts (3) is ke baad koi success record nahi hua - abhi tak. Ab hamein raw evidence mein jaa kar isay validate karna hai.

steps.title: Step 2 - Evidence Validate Karo
steps.ask: Windows Security evidence mein search karo 'EventID=4625' taake failed attempts khud dekh sako.
steps.why: Alert ko sirf maan lena kaafi nahi - hamesha raw log mein evidence dhoondo aur count khud verify karo.
steps.reveal: 7 alag 4625 events milay, sab r.malik account ke against, sab 198.51.100.23 se, 03:41:04 se 03:41:51 tak (sirf 47 second mein). Yeh bohat tez rate hai - automated tool ka sign.

steps.title: Step 3 - Asset aur Account Identify Karo
steps.ask: Account Context evidence set kholo aur dekho r.malik ka normal login pattern kya hai.
steps.why: Jab tak hamein maloom na ho ke account normally kaisay use hota hai, hum yeh nahi keh sakte ke current activity normal hai ya nahi.
steps.hintText: Account Context set mein r.malik ki row parho.
steps.reveal: r.malik ek Sales department ka normal user hai jo sirf WKS-3502 ke console (interactive) se login karta hai - is account ke liye koi legitimate remote/network logon use case configured nahi hai. Is liye SourceIP=198.51.100.23 se Type 3 (network) attempt already suspicious hai.

steps.title: Step 4 - Source IP Check Karo
steps.ask: Threat Intel Enrichment set mein 198.51.100.23 ko search karo.
steps.why: External source IP ka reputation check karna batata hai ke yeh kisi known-bad infrastructure se hai ya kisi normal office/vendor se.
steps.hintText: IP address ko search box mein paste karo.
steps.reveal: 198.51.100.23 do alag threat-intel feeds mein known scanning/credential-stuffing infrastructure ke tor par flagged hai. Yeh koi normal vendor ya office IP nahi hai.

steps.title: Step 5 - Timeline Correlate Karo
steps.ask: Ab dobara Windows Security evidence dekho - 03:41 ke attempts aur 09:03 ka successful login (4624) ke darmiyan gap par ghour karo.
steps.why: Timeline hamein batati hai ke events aapas mein connected hain ya nahi. Bara time-gap aur alag Logon Type is baat ka sign ho sakta hai ke yeh do alag ghatnayein hain.
steps.reveal: 09:03:12 ki success ek Logon Type=2 (interactive, keyboard par) hai, SourceIP khali hai - yeh r.malik khud apne desk par login kar raha hai, office hours ke start mein. Yeh 03:41 ke Type 3 external attempts se BILKUL ALAG event hai, connected nahi.

steps.title: Step 6 - Change Calendar Check Karo
steps.ask: Change Calendar / SOP evidence set kholo aur dekho kya WKS-3502 ke liye koi authorized scan ya test scheduled tha.
steps.why: Kabhi bhi 'suspicious' lagne wali activity ko True Positive kehne se pehle change calendar zaroor check karo - authorized activity accha False Positive candidate hoti hai.
steps.hintText: Change Calendar set ki pehli row parho.
steps.reveal: Change calendar mein WKS-3502 ke liye 2026-03-05 ko koi scan, test ya maintenance record nahi hai. SOP-21 saaf kehta hai: is tarah ka pattern attempted compromise mana jata hai, chahe success na bhi hui ho.

steps.title: Step 7 - Decision: True Positive, False Positive ya Authorized?
steps.ask: Ab decide karo: yeh activity True Positive hai, False Positive hai, ya Authorized Activity?
options: True Positive - attempted compromise (koi success nahi lekin still real threat)
steps.explain: Sahi jawab True Positive hai. Wajah: (1) external, threat-intel-flagged IP, (2) account ka koi legitimate remote-logon use case nahi, (3) koi change calendar entry nahi, (4) SOP-21 explicitly kehta hai success na hona bhi threat ko invalid nahi karta. r.malik ka apna 09:03 login ek totally separate, normal event hai.

steps.title: Step 8 - Escalation Decide Karo
steps.ask: Kya yeh case Tier-2 ko escalate hona chahiye, ya Tier-1 khud close kar sakta hai?
options: Tier-1 khud close kar de, koi escalation nahi chahiye
Block IP aur monitor karo, escalation sirf Tier-0 asset ke liye chahiye - yahan workstation hai to Tier-1 close kar sakta hai
IP ko block karo aur SOP ke mutabiq document karo, koi mazeed escalation abhi zaroori nahi lekin agar dobara attempt ho to turant escalate karo
steps.explain: WKS-3502 Tier-0 asset nahi hai (yeh SOP-12 ka scope nahi), is liye mandatory Tier-2 escalation zaroori nahi - lekin best practice yeh hai ke IP ko block/monitor karo, case ko True Positive ke tor par document karo, aur agar yehi source dobara try kare to escalate karo. Yeh farq samajhna zaroori hai: har True Positive automatically Tier-2 escalation nahi banta - yeh asset criticality par depend karta hai.

steps.title: Step 9 - Analyst Notes Likho
steps.ask: Ab socho tum apni Analyst Notes kaise likhoge is case ke liye.
steps.why: Achi notes agle analyst (ya khud tumhe baad mein) poori kahani samjha deti hain bina dobara sari evidence khangalay.
steps.reveal: Misal: 'r.malik (WKS-3502) par 7x failed logon (4625) 198.51.100.23 se, 03:41:04-03:41:51, Logon Type 3, SubStatus 0xC000006A. IP threat-intel par scanning/cred-stuffing infrastructure ke tor par flagged. Account ka koi remote-logon use case nahi (Account Context). Change calendar mein koi matching authorized activity nahi (SOP-21 applies). Baad ka 09:03:12 login (Type 2, interactive) unrelated normal user activity hai. Decision: True Positive - attempted compromise, koi success nahi. Action: IP block/monitor recommend kiya, escalation abhi zaroori nahi (non-Tier-0 asset), dobara attempt hone par escalate karna hai.' Ab tum Real Investigation mode ke liye ready ho - wahan ek bilkul alag scenario hai aur is baar koi answers reveal nahi hongay.

title: Windows Event Investigation

theory.concept: Directory object changes are logged as their own event family. 4720 creates a user, 4722 enables it, 4724 resets a password, 4728/4732 add a member to a global/local security group, 4738 modifies an account, 4726 deletes one. An attacker who has domain write access will usually create or promote an account, because that survives the password reset you are about to perform on the account they stole.
theory.why: Containment fails when you reset the compromised account and miss the backdoor account. Checking for account creation and group changes during the attack window is mandatory after any credential compromise.
look: 4720 followed within seconds by 4722 and 4732 from the same subject account
New accounts whose names imitate service accounts: svc_, adm_, help-desk, or a trailing character variation on a real account
Membership additions to Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Backup Operators or local Administrators
The Subject account on the event - that tells you which compromised identity performed the change
Account creation outside change-management hours
fp: IT genuinely creates accounts - always check the ticket/change reference and whether the subject is an identity-management service account
Group membership changes during onboarding batches
tips: The Subject/Caller field answers 'who did this'. The Target field answers 'to whom'.
A new account with a password that never expires and no manager attribute is a strong backdoor indicator.

title: Linux Log Investigation

theory.concept: Linux security telemetry is mostly plain text. /var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL) carries SSH and sudo activity; the systemd journal carries service events; .bash_history, cron and systemd units carry what happened after access. There are no event IDs - you grep.
theory.why: Servers, containers and network appliances are overwhelmingly Linux. An analyst who can only read Windows events is blind to half the estate.
look: 'Failed password for invalid user X' - the username does not exist, so this is enumeration
'Accepted password' or 'Accepted publickey' - note which, because password auth on a server that should be key-only is itself a finding
'session opened for user root' immediately after a suspicious accept
sudo entries with COMMAND= showing what was actually run
New SSH keys appended to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new cron entries, new systemd units
fp: Automation and monitoring accounts log in constantly from fixed internal addresses
A failed password burst from a single internal host is usually a stale credential in a script
tips: The port number in the sshd line is the attacker's source port - sequential ports across attempts mean an automated tool.
After the accept, read history and sudo before anything else: that is the actual intrusion.

title: Network Traffic Analysis

theory.concept: Flow records (NetFlow/IPFIX, firewall session logs, Zeek conn.log) summarise every connection: source, destination, port, protocol, duration, bytes in and out. You rarely get full packet capture in production, so the analyst learns to read behaviour from shape alone - how often, how long, how much, in which direction.
theory.why: Every intrusion eventually has to communicate. Flow analysis catches malware that is invisible on the endpoint because the operator is signing or obfuscating the binary.
look: Regular connection intervals with low byte counts - beaconing
Asymmetric volume: far more bytes out than in suggests exfiltration; far more in than out suggests tool download
Non-standard ports for standard protocols, or standard ports carrying the wrong protocol
Long-lived sessions (hours) to a single external address
Connections from servers that should never initiate outbound traffic
fp: Software update services, telemetry and cloud backup all produce regular outbound patterns and large uploads
Monitoring agents keep long-lived sessions open by design
tips: Compute the interval between connections yourself; jitter of a few seconds around a fixed value still means beaconing.
Bytes matter: 600 bytes every 5 minutes is a heartbeat, 400 MB in one session is a data transfer.

title: DNS Investigation

theory.concept: DNS resolution logs are the cheapest full-estate visibility a SOC has: almost every connection begins with a query, and internal resolvers see every client. Two abuse patterns dominate - algorithmically generated domains (DGA) used to rotate C2 infrastructure, and DNS tunnelling, where data is encoded into subdomain labels and answers, usually over TXT or NULL records.
theory.why: DNS tells you the blast radius. One infected host is an incident; forty resolving the same domain is a campaign.
look: High query volume to a single parent domain with long, random-looking subdomain labels
TXT or NULL record types where an application has no business using them
Newly registered domains - creation date within days of first resolution
Queries to a domain from hosts that share nothing else in common
NXDOMAIN storms - a DGA cycling through candidate domains until one is live
fp: Content delivery networks, antivirus cloud lookups and some VPN clients legitimately use long hashed labels and TXT records
Email security (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) checks are TXT queries by design
tips: Count distinct clients per suspicious domain before you decide severity.
Domain age is decisive evidence: a C2 domain registered nine days ago is not a CDN.
